game.title: ROCKSLIDE: Mountain Patrol
game.pitch: You are Vince, twenty, long blonde hair with a bit of a curl, the newest hand on the Kessel Patrol. You run the mountain patrol for the Kessel valley: its slopes, its roads, its village and the people who get lost on it. You have a log station, a snowmobile, a helicopter, a pair of old skis, and Koda, a grey-and-white husky with one ear that never stands up.

unclassified.doc:
`ahead`: how far past the character the camera aims, as a share of its distance. Aiming past
you rather than at you puts you in the lower third and shows the ground you are heading into.
`portrait`: how much further back the camera sits on a tall, narrow phone screen.

Each piece's footprint (its own frame, metres) and how it meets the ground. `rules` say what ground it
can stand on when its spot is chosen; `drape` is how high (local y) the ground snow it carries reaches:
those parts are laid onto the terrain under them rather than left flat.

The ground: snow that is a little blue in the shade and warm in the sun, wind-scoured rock on
the steeps, packed roads, groomed pistes and the lake's grey ice. Drawn in chunks so the ones
behind you are culled; a ring of far peaks closes the valley.
Hand-placed patrol props: a rescue toboggan at the station, the lift top and the base; rescue caches where trouble happens; lanterns by doors.

missions.brief: The weather station up on Grauhorn Pass went quiet overnight. Take the sled up the pass road and get it talking again. Koda will want to come.

missions.title: Controlled Release

missions.title: Lost on the Tannberg
missions.brief: Nils Brandt, 34, skied off the back of the Tannberg top station into the trees and has not come down. His phone is dead. His friends found one of his gloves by the lift. Get Koda on his scent.

objectives.text: Load the supply crate onto the sled rack

levelcraft.title: LEVELCRAFT

findings.title: 56% of the mapped area holds nothing to find or do
findings.summary: Dividing the playable extent (1720×1305 units) into a 6×6 grid, 20 cells contain no placed location and no mission target; the emptiest quarter is the north-east (6 of 9 cells empty).
findings.why: Players read empty space as either a promise or a waste. Without a landmark, a cache or a reason to cross it, a large empty area becomes travel time between the parts of the game that matter.

evidence.text: 62 positioned locations and targets; 20 empty grid cells
evidence.symbol: positions across CHARGE_SPOTS, GROVES, PADS, PEAKS, SHELVES

findings.title: 20 of 45 named places are never a mission destination
findings.summary: No mission objective targets Tannberg Base, Fernhut Cabin, Slope A, Slope B, Slope C and 15 more. They exist in the world data but the mission structure never asks the player to go there.
findings.why: Named places are authored promises. When no objective, story beat or reward points at them, most players never discover they exist, and the world feels smaller than the map.

evidence.text: Tannberg Base (PADS) is not targeted by any of 8 missions
Fernhut Cabin (PADS) is not targeted by any of 8 missions
Slope A (CHARGE_SPOTS) is not targeted by any of 8 missions
Slope B (CHARGE_SPOTS) is not targeted by any of 8 missions
Slope C (CHARGE_SPOTS) is not targeted by any of 8 missions
Slope D (CHARGE_SPOTS) is not targeted by any of 8 missions

strengths: 11 kinds of place across 45 named locations (variety 0.78).

missioncraft.title: MISSIONCRAFT

findings.title: 'interact' is 37% of all objectives
findings.summary: 13 of 35 objectives use the verb 'interact'.
findings.why: One verb doing most of the work makes the mission set feel like one mission with different names.

evidence.text: Morning Rounds: Say good morning to Koda
Morning Rounds: Clear the ice off the station and restart it
Controlled Release: Take the charges from the locker in the garage
Controlled Release: Close the pass road at the barrier
Controlled Release: Reopen the pass road

findings.title: 2 missions share the same structure: travel → interact
findings.summary: Tree Down on the Pass and Stuck in the Drift have an identical sequence of objective types. 2 of 8 missions repeat a structure another mission already uses.
findings.why: When the structure repeats, players stop reading the brief: they already know what will happen. The fiction changes, the decisions do not.

evidence.text: Tree Down on the Pass: goto → interact
Stuck in the Drift: goto → interact

findings.title: Only 0 of 35 objectives offer more than one way to complete them
findings.summary: Almost every objective has exactly one target and one method in its definition.
findings.why: Alternate solutions are where players express themselves. Without them, skill shows only as speed, and every player has the same story to tell.

evidence.text: Morning Rounds: Say good morning to Koda (one target)
Morning Rounds: Get on the sled in the garage (one target)
Morning Rounds: Ride up the pass road to the weather station (one target)
Morning Rounds: Clear the ice off the station and restart it (one target)
Morning Rounds: Head home to the station (one target)

findings.title: No optional or bonus objectives
findings.summary: None of the 35 objectives is marked optional or bonus.
findings.why: Optional objectives let experts set their own bar and give curious players a reason to linger without forcing everyone to.

evidence.text: 8 missions; 0 objectives with optional/bonus fields

findings.title: Missions define no way to fail
findings.summary: No mission definition has a fail condition, time limit or loss state; the source has 12 fail-state references, so failure may live in code outside the mission data.
findings.why: Stakes come from the possibility of losing something. Without a fail state, tension is only implied by the fiction, and players learn they can ignore it.

evidence.text: 8 mission definitions, 0 with fail/timer/limit fields

strengths: 5 mission families; response (3), community (2), recon (1), avalanche (1), rescue (1).
funds rewards scale with effort (rank correlation 0.78).
Missions grow from 5.0 to 6.0 objectives on average as they unlock.

storycraft.title: STORYCRAFT

findings.title: One story path: no endings, choices or branches in the data
findings.summary: No ending definitions and no scripted choices were found, although the docs talk about choice or consequence 15 times.
findings.why: A fixed story is fine when it is the point. When the docs promise consequence, players will look for the fork and find none.

evidence.text: 0 endings, 0 choices in data; 15 doc mentions of choice/consequence

findings.title: 5 of 8 missions mention no character
findings.summary: The briefs, objectives and completion text of Eyes on Kessel Bowl, Controlled Release, Firewood for the Kettle, Tree Down on the Pass and 1 more name none of the 7 characters.
findings.why: Players care about outcomes for people. A mission with nobody in it is a chore, however good the verbs are.

evidence.text: Eyes on Kessel Bowl: no character named
Controlled Release: no character named
Firewood for the Kettle: no character named
Tree Down on the Pass: no character named
Stuck in the Drift: no character named

strengths: 7 speaking characters; most lines: dispatch (10), avalanche (9), greta (6).

progressioncraft.title: PROGRESSIONCRAFT

findings.title: Buying everything costs 5.1× what the campaign pays
findings.summary: The non-repeating missions pay 1390 funds in total; the 35 priced unlocks cost 7100. The gap is meant to be filled by 2 repeatable mission(s) (Tree Down on the Pass and Stuck in the Drift).
findings.why: A large gap between income and prices turns the late game into grinding. If repeatable content fills it, that content carries the game's pacing and must be the best-designed part.

evidence.text: campaign income 1390 funds
35 priced entries, 50–520

strengths: Replay sources: repeatable missions (2), randomness (200), procedural (7), best scores (107), seeded (95).

experiencecraft.title: EXPERIENCECRAFT

findings.title: The player decides how fast, never what or how
findings.summary: No objective offers alternatives, none is optional, and the story has no endings or choices in the data; free play exists (12 references) but is separate from the missions.
findings.why: Agency is the difference between playing a game and operating it. Players who cannot choose anything that matters stop forming intentions of their own.

evidence.text: agency sources: {'alternative_objectives': 0, 'optional_objectives': 0, 'endings': 0, 'choices': 0, 'free_play_signals': 12}

findings.title: PLAYCRAFT measured 5.1 s from load to first input
findings.summary: In PLAYCRAFT run 20261105001110-pass-06bc6f6e the game took 5.1 s before it accepted play (software renderer; real devices are usually faster).
findings.why: The first seconds decide whether a mobile player stays. Anything between tap and play should be part of the experience, not a wait.
